items.title: 20.2.1 Tools used in Recombinant DNA Technology

source_refs.note: Topic 20.2.1 with the For Information box (PDF 156-157); Figure 20.1 is replaced by the original diagram.

blocks.text: The gene of interest is the gene to be manipulated. It can be obtained in three ways.

items: Direct synthesis in the laboratory using enzymes such as polymerases and ligases.
Synthesis from its mRNA by reverse transcription, using the enzyme reverse transcriptase.
Cutting it out of a chromosome with restriction endonucleases.

blocks.text: These enzymes, the 'molecular scissors', cut specific nucleotide sequences in DNA. Each kind recognises its own sequence, the restriction site or recognition region, binds there and cuts the DNA at a particular place within it. Restriction sites are palindromic sequences of four to eight nucleotides: the nucleotides at one end are complementary to those at the other, so the two strands read the same sequence in opposite directions. The enzyme cuts both strands, leaving both fragments with single-stranded ends a few nucleotides long that are complementary to each other, the sticky ends.

blocks.alt: A long DNA duplex with two recognition sites, GAATTC on the top strand and CTTAAG on the bottom strand. Triangles mark the cut between G and A on each strand. A green arrow labelled 'Action of enzyme' leads to three fragments: the middle piece has single-stranded AATT overhangs at both ends, and the end pieces have matching overhangs.
blocks.caption: Figure 20.1: Action of restriction endonuclease (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 20.1).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Recognition sites, DNA duplex, Restriction endonuclease, Action of enzyme, Single-stranded sticky ends.

blocks.title: For information
blocks.text: Restriction endonucleases are valuable because any two DNA fragments produced by the same restriction endonuclease can be joined together.

Vectors, or molecular carriers, take the gene of interest into host cells: the gene is attached to the vector, which becomes recombinant DNA, and the rDNA is put into the host cells. Bacterial plasmids are the most commonly used.

items: Bacteriophages, such as phage lambda and bacteriophage P1.
Cosmids: plasmids that contain a small region of bacteriophage DNA called the cos sequence.
P1 artificial chromosomes, with features of both P1 vectors and BACs.
Animal viruses, such as a human cold virus, to carry genes into monkey and human cells.

blocks.alt: Source DNA with the gene of interest (pink) between two cut sites is cut by a restriction endonuclease into pieces with stepped ends, releasing the gene of interest. A ring-shaped vector (plasmid) is cut by the same enzyme into a cleaved vector. The gene of interest goes into the cleaved vector, and the two join into a ring of recombinant DNA.
blocks.caption: Figure 20.2: Use of Vector (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 20.2).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Restriction endonuclease, Gene of interest, Vector (Plasmid), Cleaved Vector, Recombinant DNA.

blocks.text: DNA ligase joins two DNA fragments, so it is called molecular glue: it forms the phosphodiester linkage between two adjacent nucleotides.

An expression system is a suitable organism that can host the rDNA and express the gene of interest; the choice depends on the vector used. Bacterial cells are ideal because of their short generation time and simple genetic system.
